theDefectTheVIOLATIONPROBEFOUND.what: The first implementation derived `provenance.parcelJoin.state` and `featureIndex` from the OFFERED crosswalk row while every geometry consumer read a separate `row` variable. Disabling the `row = crosswalkRow` assignment left the payload claiming `joined-crosswalk` at feature 40337 while drawing feature 57725 -- a provenance record describing a bind that did not happen, which is worse than either outcome alone.
theDefectTheVIOLATIONPROBEFOUND.howItWasFound: by violating the change, not by reading it. The first probe made only ONE test fail and the shape of that single failure is what exposed it.
theDefectTheVIOLATIONPROBEFOUND.fix: the record is now derived from `crosswalkBound = crosswalkRow != null && row === crosswalkRow`, so the state can only claim a bind the geometry actually took.
theDefectTheVIOLATIONPROBEFOUND.regressionControl: a test that reads the geometry side (the zoning stamp, which exists on only one of the two features) and the provenance side and asserts they agree. Re-running the same violation now fails 5 tests instead of 1.

theSecondDefectTheVIOLATIONPROBEFOUND.what: The parser test for the honest-null case asserted only that `HeaderIndex.get` returns "" for a missing column. That is a presence-shaped check on the wrong layer: replacing `textOrNull(header.get(...))` with the raw `header.get(...)` in the parser left the test PASSING while every row of such a county acquired an empty-string identifier -- a sentinel that satisfies a not-null check, identifies nothing, and would become a join key every row in the county shared.
theSecondDefectTheVIOLATIONPROBEFOUND.fix: a real fixture (lib/cad-ingest/src/__tests__/__fixtures__/orion_no_identifier_columns_sample.csv, a property-classified header with neither column) run THROUGH the parser, asserting null on both. The same violation now fails.

twoDesignDECISIONSthatChangedUnderMeasur.what: the migration originally carried a partial index on (county_fips, property_number). REMOVED.
twoDesignDECISIONSthatChangedUnderMeasur.why: two reasons, and the second is the one that matters. Nothing queries cad_property by property_number -- the bake loads the county's declared-vintage rows by (county_fips, tax_year) and reads the column off rows it already has, so the index is an artifact that exists, is correct, and does nothing. And this repo's schema fixture is a pg_dump of what `drizzle-kit push` builds from the DRIZZLE SCHEMA, not of what the migrations build. Proven, not assumed: migration 0095's txgio_parcel.geom column AND txgio_parcel_geom_gist_idx are in that migration and live in production and appear NOWHERE in schema.sql.template. A migration-only index would therefore have drifted the fixture and failed CI's own drift check.

twoDesignDECISIONSthatChangedUnderMeasur.what: the geo_id fetch originally compared `btrim(geo_id) = ANY(...)`. Now compares the raw column.
twoDesignDECISIONSthatChangedUnderMeasur.why: measured: ZERO of Hays' 130,246 non-null geo_ids carry surrounding whitespace, so trimming the comparand changes no result and would permanently prevent a plain (county_fips, geo_id) index from being used. txgio_parcel has no geo_id index today and the situs join already pays that price -- it needed a 34-call functional index to escape it. The blank guard stays. If a publisher ever pads a geo_id the failure is a MISS, which is an honest geometry absence, never a wrong bind.
twoDesignDECISIONSthatChangedUnderMeasur.cost: measured on staging: one 5,000-key chunk takes 4.3 seconds without an index, so Hays' 115,035 keys are roughly 24 chunks and about 100 seconds of the bake. Named so the integration seat is not surprised.
